title: CBA may buy back share in Colonial First State
full_text:
Speculation is mounting that the country’s largest mortgage holder CBA could be moving to buy back the share it no longer owns in Colonial First State from Kohlberg Kravis Roberts after offers for the business did not live up to its $5bn-plus price expectations.
DataRoom reported that Brookfield, advised by Citi, had been eyeing the business, but the understanding is it failed to reach CFS’s price expectations and stopped working on a transaction.
Now there’s chatter that CBA may take all of Colonial First State back in house. The logic for the move, according to sources, is that CBA achieved a strong price for a 55 per cent interest in the business when it was sold to KKR in 2020 for $1.7bn.
DataRoom understands that after the top four banks retreated from the wealth management space following a royal commission into the industry and sold off their wealth management operations, they were now keen on buying businesses in that sector again.
It comes in the context of softening conditions in the housing market and higher interest rates, which means the country’s major lenders are searching for new growth avenues.
Westpac had its wealth management platform BT Panorama on the market, but then opted to retain it, while NAB is expected to retain wealth manager JB Were, despite fielding numerous approaches from interested buyers.
A CFS sale process has been run by Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Barrenjoey and it is believed the asking price has been about $5bn.
The master trust is understood to represent the majority of CFS’s value, while some had earlier considered that its smaller CFS Edge business could be of interest to some parties.
It also has managed accounts and portfolios.
Some market experts have questioned whether CBA would meet KKR’s price expectations for a stake in the business. One source said a motivating factor for a purchase would be preventing the business being tipped by KKR into a continuation fund if a sale did not come through, which would not be the bank’s preference.
